To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The Macondo well oil spilled into the water column was transported to the seaflood in the months following the blowout and (2) the oil was deposited on the seabed in the form of a thin oil layer, which was later resuspended and/or biodegraded.
the hydrocarbons from the Macondo blowout sedimented to the seabed in subsequent months, and that the concentrations of oil and its biomarkers decreased in the following years.
sedimented hydrocarbons from the 2010 Macondo well accident were still present in the Gulf of Mexic
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fate of oil in the Gulf of México after the Macondo oil spill.
the distribution, composition, and sources of hydrocarbons in sediments in the vicinity of the Macondo oil spill in the Gulf of Mexcio, and the fate of the hydrocarbons in the sediment.
the hydrocarbon composition and concentrations of the Gulf of Mexico (GOM) surface and sub-surface sediments in the three years following the Maconda well blowout.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Macondo oil spill impacted the seafloor and that its effects are still visible today.
the Macondo oil spill had a limited impact on the seabed of the northern Gulf of México, and the observed hydrocarbon concentrations were not significantly different from the pre-spill conditions.
a substantial amount of the Macondo oil sedimented to the seabed, but that the majority of it has been lost to the environment by the end of the 2013 sampling period.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Macondo oil spill did not have a lasting effect on the seafloor sediments in the northern Gulf.
the oil from the Macondo blowout did reach the seafloor and that the concentrations of oil on the seabed were highest in late 2010 and early 2011.
there was no clear trend of increasing or decreasing hydrocarbon concentrations in the subsurface sediments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the hydrocarbon concentrations in surface sediments were highest in the late summer/early fall of 2010 (when oil was still present in the water column) and decreased in the following years.
the Macondo oil is still present on the seafloor 3 years after the blowout.

the hydrocarbon composition and concentrations of surface sediments are useful indicators of the fate of hydrocarbons in the environment, particularly when combined with the results from water column and other sediment samples.
